questions.q: Why does this lesson say monitoring only Salesforce's own health signals can be misleading for an enterprise process?
options: Because Salesforce's health signals are always inaccurate
Because an order can look perfectly healthy inside Salesforce while actually having failed on the receiving system (like the ERP) for reasons Salesforce never saw
Because Salesforce does not generate any health signals at all
Because monitoring is unnecessary once a process has been tested once
questions.explain: The lesson's key example is an opportunity closing and an integration call firing successfully inside Salesforce, while the ERP silently rejects the order on its end -- Salesforce-only monitoring shows green lights on a process that actually failed.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the real scope of Salesforce's Event Monitoring?
options: It monitors every connected external system's internal processing automatically
It replaces the need for any end-to-end observability design
It only logs activity that occurs in a sandbox, never in production
It logs detailed user and system activity inside Salesforce, but its visibility stops at Salesforce's own boundary
questions.explain: Event Monitoring logs activity (logins, API calls, exports) inside Salesforce specifically, but it can't see what a downstream system like the ERP did with data after receiving it -- its visibility stops at Salesforce's own boundary.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a 'correlation ID' is used for?
options: Encrypting a field's value at rest
Assigning a classification tier to a dataset
A shared tracking identifier that travels with a business transaction across every system it touches, letting its full journey be reconstructed from logs scattered across systems
Identifying which sandbox type a given org uses
questions.explain: A correlation ID is a shared identifier attached to a business transaction as it moves across multiple systems, allowing its end-to-end journey to be reconstructed from each system's separate logs when something goes wrong.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what operational failure happens when an alert 'routes to the wrong place'?
options: The alert is automatically duplicated across every team in the company
The alert disappears entirely and is never logged anywhere
The issue resolves itself automatically without anyone needing to act
A failure is technically visible in one system's logs but invisible to or not understood by the team actually responsible for the business impact, so it goes unaddressed
questions.explain: The lesson describes a batch sync failure that technically lives in the integration platform's logs but doesn't reach the team that understands its business consequence (like the sales team losing visibility into order status) -- an alert that exists but reaches no one who can act on it.

questions.q: What does this lesson say end-to-end observability requires, beyond any single Salesforce feature?
options: Nothing extra -- Salesforce's native monitoring tools already cover every system in the integration chain
A deliberate architectural discipline designed by the System Architect, since no individual system's native monitoring is built to see across a boundary it doesn't own
Disabling Event Monitoring entirely in favor of a third-party tool
Only applies to companies running a multi-org Salesforce architecture
questions.explain: The lesson states end-to-end observability is an architectural discipline the System Architect has to design deliberately -- things like logging rejection details, tracking event consumption downstream, and correlation IDs -- because no single system's native tool sees across a boundary it doesn't own.
